ROCOR parish sources

6 sectionsNot completed
Notes

These resources distinguish a historical service book from the publications of particular ROCOR communities. ROCOR means the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia; the named parish, monastery and diocesan sources retain their own settings.[1][5]

For whom did Hapgood prepare her service book?[1]

Hapgood says she worked primarily for the Russian Church in America and used its Church Slavonic books while comparing them with the Greek. She distinguishes differences of arrangement and practice from differences of dogma, meaning doctrine. This explains the particular background of the edition used throughout these lessons.[1]

Read original passage

Hapgood’s stated scope

I have used the Old Church-Slavonic books of the Russian Church, rather than the original Greek, because my work has been done, prima- rily, for the use of the Russian Church in America. Slight differences in arrangement and practice (not in dogma) have arisen between the Russian Church and the Greek Church, similar to those between the Church of England and the Protestant Episcopal Church in America. I have carefully compared everything with the original Greek.

Why can printed books and parish practice differ?[1]

Hapgood states that some things said or done by custom are not recorded in the printed books. She therefore describes editorial selection as well as translation. The observation identifies the limits of using one published book as an exhaustive account of lived church practice.[1]

Read original passage

Published books and custom

It will be seen that I have been confronted with the problem of re- jection, as well as of judicious selection. I may add, that many things are done or said "by custom " which are not mentioned in the printed books. These I have included.

A parish’s Communion guidance[2]

The linked St Matrona Orthodox Mission page identifies that parish’s guidance concerning Communion. It is a local source rather than a preparation rule written by the app.[2]

A monastery’s service schedule[3]

The linked Holy Trinity Monastery page is its published service schedule. The monastery’s current publication is the source for actual times, rather than a timetable copied into this lesson.[3]

A publication about preparing the calendar[4]

This linked account concerns preparation of the ROCOR liturgical calendar. It identifies how a particular calendar publication is discussed without replacing the current calendar itself.[4]

A published akathist[5]

The linked ROCOR Europe page contains an akathist to the Theotokos, the Mother of God. An akathist is a particular hymn form; the prayer text and its order belong to that named publication.[5]
